title: Why June brings polar day to Tromsø and winter to Sydney

steps.title: The axis keeps its direction all year
steps.line: At 23.44°, north leans sunward in June and away in December.
steps.caption: Earth’s axis is tilted 23.44° from the normal to its orbit and points the same way all year, so the north end leans toward the Sun in June and away from it in December. Sizes and distances are not to scale.
steps.picture: An orbit around the Sun, not to scale; Earth in June (right), September (top), December (left) and March (bottom), its axis tilted the same way each time.

steps.title: June: Tromsø’s noon Sun at 43.8°
steps.line: The lit part of Tromsø’s circle gives 24.0 h of daylight.
steps.caption: In June the north end leans toward the Sun far enough that Tromsø’s whole latitude circle sits on the day side. As Earth turns, Tromsø never enters the night half, so the Sun stays up for all 24 hours.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; 1 label.

steps.title: June noon: the Sun stands 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon
steps.caption: Zoomed in on the red dot. The white line is Tromsø’s horizon, and noon sunlight arrives parallel to the Sun’s direction. The angle between them is 90° minus the gap between the latitude, 69.65°, and the latitude where the June Sun is overhead, 23.44°.
steps.picture: Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; Close-up on Tromsø at noon in June: its horizon, the noon sunlight, and the 43.8° angle between them, 90° − |69.65° − 23.44°| = 43.79°. New in this step: Close-up on Tromsø at noon in June: its horizon, the noon sunlight, and the 43.8° angle between them, 90° − |69.65° − 23.44°| = 43.79°.

steps.title: December: the same axis, Tromsø’s Sun at -3.1°
steps.line: The south end leans sunward; daylight goes 24.0 h to 0.0 h.
steps.caption: Half an orbit later Earth is on the far side of the Sun, but the axis still points the same way, so the south end now leans sunward and the hemispheres swap seasons. Under the globes, Tromsø’s daylight drops from 24.0 h in June to 0.0 h.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; Earth in December from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, stopped by the globe: below Tromsø’s horizon; 2 labels. New in this step: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in December from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, stopped by the globe: below Tromsø’s horizon; and 1 more.

steps.title: Latitude sets how much of each circle is lit
steps.line: Tromsø’s circle is all lit in June; the equator’s is half lit.
steps.caption: Each line is one place’s latitude circle, yellow where it is in daylight. Tromsø’s circle is all day in June and all night in December, while the equator’s is always cut in half. The model’s day length in hours is acos(−tan latitude × tan declination) in degrees, divided by 7.5.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; Earth in December from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, stopped by the globe: below Tromsø’s horizon; The other places’ latitude circles on both views, yellow where lit; “June”, 4 labelled values; “December”, 4 labelled values. Marked: Tromsø: 24.0 h; Tromsø: 0.0 h. New in this step: The other places’ latitude circles on both views, yellow where lit; “June”, 4 labelled values; “December”, 4 labelled values.

steps.title: A computed year of daylight in Tromsø
steps.line: 24 h for 60 days, 0 h for 61; 12 h at the equinoxes.
steps.caption: The curve samples the same model through the year, with the Sun’s declination on each day. It stays flat at 24 hours for 60 days around the June solstice, the span the dimension marks, when Tromsø’s whole circle is lit, and at 0 for 61 days around December; both counts run the model on all 365 days. Every place gets 12 hours at the two equinoxes.
steps.picture: A chart of daylight in hours, 0 to 24, through the months January to December; Tromsø’s daylight through the year, from 0.0 h to 24.0 h, flat at 24 h for 60 days and at 0 h for 61; Dashed lines at the March and September equinoxes and the June and December solstices; The curve’s value on those days: Mar equinox 12.0 h, Jun solstice 24.0 h, Sep equinox 12.0 h, Dec solstice 0.0 h; A dimension line marked “60 days”; 1 label.

steps.title: Earth is nearest the Sun in January, during the northern winter
steps.line: 15 January: Tromsø gets 0.0 h, latitude -69.7° gets 24.0 h.
steps.caption: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January. On 15 January Tromsø gets 0.0 h of daylight and latitude -69.7°, the second curve, gets 24.0 h. Both are the same distance from the Sun that day, so the opposite seasons must come from the tilt.
steps.picture: A chart of daylight in hours, 0 to 24, through the months January to December; Tromsø’s daylight through the year, from 0.0 h to 24.0 h, flat at 24 h for 60 days and at 0 h for 61; 15 January marked on the chart at 0.0 h; The same model at latitude -69.7°, Tromsø’s curve turned upside down: 24.0 h on 15 January; An exaggerated orbit: Earth nearest the Sun in January, farthest in July; Beside the 15 January dots: Tromsø 0.0 h, latitude -69.7° 24.0 h. steps.title: The same formula draws all four daylight curves
steps.line: London and Sydney peak six months apart; Quito stays at 12 h.
steps.caption: The chart runs the same model at four latitudes. Tromsø’s curve sits flat at 24 h and at 0 h for weeks, London and Sydney peak six months apart, and Quito stays at 12 hours.
